title: Angioid Streaks: The Cracks in Bruch's Membrane
summary: Angioid streaks are irregular, jagged, tapering lines radiating from the peripapillary region, resulting from dehiscences in a calcified and brittle Bruch's membrane. This visual guide explores their systemic associations, clinical presentation, and management.

content.explanation: P: Pseudoxanthoma Elasticum (PXE); E: Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome; P: Paget Disease of Bone; S: Sickle Cell Disease (and other hemoglobinopathies); I: Idiopathic.

sections.title: Clinical Features & Signs
content: Irregular, jagged, reddish-brown to dark gray lines
Tapering appearance away from the optic disc
Peau d'orange: Mottled RPE appearance (often precedes streaks)
Optic Disc Drusen: Frequently seen in PXE patients

rows: Grönblad-Strandberg syndrome; 'plucked chicken skin' appearance; most common cause.
Type VI (Ocular-scoliotic form); joint hypermobility; skin hyperextensibility.
Increased bone turnover; 1-2% of patients develop angioid streaks.
HbSS, HbSC, and Thalassemia; vascular occlusions.
Pituitary tumors, Lead poisoning, Hyperphosphatemia, Hypercalcinosis.

sections.title: Major Complications
content: Choroidal Neovascularization (CNV): Leading cause of vision loss
Subretinal Hemorrhage: Can occur after trivial blunt trauma
Foveal Involvement: Direct extension of a streak into the macula
Disciform Scarring: Resulting from untreated CNV

rows: High myopia; usually horizontal; no peripapillary radiating pattern.
History of trauma; concentric to the optic disc; usually white/yellow.
Atrophic scars with pigmented borders; inflammatory history.
Posterior staphyloma; tilted disc; lacquer cracks.

sections.title: Diagnostic Evaluation
content: Fundus Fluorescein Angiography (FFA): Streaks show 'window defects' (hyperfluorescence) or staining.
Indocyanine Green Angiography (ICGA): May reveal more extensive streaks than clinical exam.
Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT): Detects intraretinal or subretinal fluid (CNV).
Autofluorescence: Streaks often appear hypo-autofluorescent with hyper-autofluorescent borders.

sections.title: Management & Patient Education
content: Step 1: Baseline documentation with fundus photography and OCT.
Step 2: Home monitoring with Amsler grid to detect early CNV.
Step 3: Strict use of safety glasses (polycarbonate) during sports to prevent trauma-induced hemorrhage.
Step 4: Intravitreal Anti-VEGF therapy if CNV develops.
Step 5: Systemic workup for associated diseases (Cardiology, Dermatology, Genetics).

sections.title: Verbatim Clinical Summary
sections.content: Angioid streaks are characterized by a crack-like appearance of the fundus due to changes in Bruch's membrane. While the streaks themselves are often asymptomatic, they predispose the eye to choroidal neovascularization and extreme sensitivity to trauma. Clinical management focuses on the early detection of neovascular complications and the identification of potentially serious systemic underlying conditions such as Pseudoxanthoma Elasticum or Paget's Disease.
